name: Securities & Investments
notes: Competency areas taken from the 2025-26 National FBLA Securities & Investments study guide (PDF mirror: https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Securities-and-Investments.pdf; the fbla.org page returned 403 so the official host could not be confirmed). The guide lists 9 knowledge areas. Its test-composition chart is unlabelled and its bar order does not match the list, so the per-area question counts here are an approximation. Official sample items are in CONNECT and were not accessible. UK-only items in the guide (ISAs, FSMA, Data Protection Act 1998) were skipped; U.S. law and tax conventions are used throughout.

questions.q: An investor who needs her money in two years and cannot accept a loss should prioritize which investment objective?
questions.explain: A short horizon and low loss tolerance point to capital preservation. The trap is choosing growth-oriented options that carry large drawdown risk.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the risk-return tradeoff?
choices: Higher expected return generally requires accepting higher risk
Low-risk investments always produce the highest returns
Risk and expected return are unrelated for diversified portfolios
Holding cash eliminates all investment risk
questions.explain: Investors are compensated for bearing additional risk with higher expected returns, though outcomes are not guaranteed.

questions.q: Diversification across many unrelated securities primarily reduces which type of risk?
questions.explain: Company-specific risk is diversifiable. Market-wide risk remains after diversification, which is the trap.

questions.q: What is the value at the end of 2 years of $1,000 invested at 8% per year, compounded annually?
questions.explain: 1,000 x 1.08 x 1.08 = $1,166.40. The trap is simple interest, which gives $1,160.

questions.q: Using the rule of 72, approximately how many years does it take an investment earning 6% per year to double?
questions.explain: 72 divided by 6 is 12. The rule is an approximation for compounding at a constant rate.

questions.q: Which investor can generally take on the most short-term price volatility?
choices: A retiree who depends on portfolio withdrawals next month
A 64-year-old who needs all savings within 12 months
A household saving for a down payment due next year
A 30-year-old saving for retirement 35 years away
questions.explain: A long time horizon gives time to recover from short-term declines, so volatility is more tolerable.

questions.q: What is the present value of $500 received one year from now, discounted at 5% per year?
questions.explain: 500 / 1.05 = $476.19. The trap is compounding forward to $525.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most liquid asset?
questions.explain: Money market fund shares can usually be redeemed quickly at close to their stated value. The others take time or a discount to sell.

questions.q: An investment earns a 7% nominal return in a year when inflation is 3%. What is the exact real return?
questions.explain: The exact real return is (1.07 / 1.03) - 1 = 3.88%. Subtracting inflation gives the 4% approximation, which is the trap.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of dollar-cost averaging?
choices: It guarantees a higher return than lump-sum investing
It spreads purchases over time, reducing the impact of a poorly timed entry
questions.explain: Regular fixed-dollar purchases reduce the risk of investing everything at a market peak. It does not guarantee a better return.

questions.q: Which statement about a Roth IRA is correct under current U.S. federal rules?
choices: Contributions are deductible and withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income
Contributions are made with after-tax dollars and qualified withdrawals are tax-free
Contributions are deductible but withdrawals are always penalty-free
Earnings are taxed annually as they accrue
questions.explain: Roth contributions are not deducted, so qualified distributions of contributions and earnings are not taxed again.

questions.q: To qualify as a long-term capital gain for U.S. tax purposes, an asset must be held for more than:
questions.explain: Holding for more than one year gives long-term treatment. Holding for exactly one year does not qualify.

questions.q: Under the U.S. wash sale rule, a loss on a sale is disallowed if a substantially identical security is bought within:
choices: 30 days before or after the sale
questions.explain: The window is 30 days on each side of the sale, a 61-day span in total.

questions.q: Qualified dividends are generally taxed at:
questions.explain: Qualified dividends get the lower long-term capital gains rates if the holding-period rules are met.

questions.q: Earnings in a 529 college savings plan grow:
choices: Tax-free, but withdrawals are always taxed
Tax-deferred, and qualified education withdrawals are federally tax-free
Only in cash equivalents with no tax benefit
questions.explain: Growth is tax-deferred and qualified education withdrawals are federally tax-free. Non-qualified withdrawals are taxed on earnings.

questions.q: A revocable living trust generally:
choices: Lets the grantor amend or revoke it, and the assets remain in the grantor's taxable estate
Removes assets from the grantor's estate immediately and permanently
Requires the trustee to be a bank
Gives creditor protection from the grantor's personal debts
questions.explain: Because the grantor keeps control, the assets are generally still part of the taxable estate. The trap is assuming a trust always removes assets from the estate.

questions.q: Interest from most U.S. municipal bonds is generally exempt from:
choices: Capital gains tax on a sale at a profit
questions.explain: Muni interest is usually federally tax-exempt. Gains on selling a muni at a profit are still taxable.

questions.q: When an heir inherits appreciated stock, the cost basis is generally:
choices: The fair market value at the date of death
The average price over the last year
questions.explain: The basis steps up to fair market value at death, which often eliminates tax on gains that built up before death.

questions.q: In a traditional 401(k), pre-tax contributions are later taxed how?
choices: Withdrawals are tax-free after five years
Contributions are taxed when made, but withdrawals are not
Withdrawals are taxed at long-term capital gains rates
Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income
questions.explain: The contributions were never taxed, so withdrawals are ordinary income. Capital gains rates do not apply to these distributions.

questions.q: An investor in the 32% federal bracket can buy a municipal bond yielding 4% tax-free. Its tax-equivalent yield is closest to:
questions.explain: Tax-equivalent yield = 4% / (1 - 0.32) = 5.88%. Multiplying by 0.68 gives 2.72%, which is the trap.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes an ETF from a traditional open-end mutual fund?
choices: ETFs are priced once daily at NAV only
ETFs trade intraday on an exchange at market prices
ETFs cannot be held in a brokerage account
questions.explain: ETF shares trade throughout the day like stocks. Open-end mutual funds are bought and redeemed at the end-of-day NAV.

questions.q: Money market mutual funds seek to maintain a stable net asset value of:
questions.explain: Money market funds target a stable $1.00 NAV. The NAV is not guaranteed, though.

questions.q: Bank certificates of deposit are generally insured by the FDIC up to:
choices: $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category
There is no FDIC coverage on CDs
questions.explain: The standard limit is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.

questions.q: Who bears the investment risk in a variable annuity?
choices: The insurer, which guarantees all returns
The U.S. government through the FDIC
questions.explain: In a variable annuity, returns depend on the chosen subaccounts, so the owner bears the market risk. Insurance guarantees are limited.

questions.q: To keep its REIT status under U.S. tax law, a REIT must distribute at least what percent of taxable income to shareholders?
questions.explain: The statutory requirement is 90% of taxable income, which is the figure most often confused with other thresholds.

questions.q: As a target-date fund approaches its target date, its asset allocation typically:
choices: Moves entirely to cash on the first day
questions.explain: This shift is called the glide path. The fund becomes more conservative as the investor's time horizon shortens.

questions.q: Closed-end fund shares trade at a price that can differ from their net asset value. This is best described as:
choices: A premium or discount to NAV
questions.explain: Closed-end funds trade on exchanges at market prices, so they often trade at a premium or discount to NAV.

questions.q: A unit investment trust (UIT) is typically characterized by:
choices: An open-ended share count with daily NAV
A managed portfolio that changes monthly
A fixed portfolio that terminates at a set date
questions.explain: A UIT holds a fixed, unmanaged portfolio and dissolves at a stated termination date.

questions.q: Under SEC Regulation D, an individual generally qualifies as an accredited investor with net worth over:
questions.explain: The net-worth test excludes the primary residence. The income test is a separate route to accredited status.

questions.q: A 2x daily-leveraged ETF held through several volatile months will most likely:
choices: Return exactly twice the index's cumulative return
Diverge from twice the index's cumulative return because daily rebalancing compounds
Return half the index's cumulative return
questions.explain: Daily resetting compounds returns, so the multi-period result can differ substantially from 2x the index over longer holding periods.

questions.q: Preferred stock typically differs from common stock because it:
choices: Has unlimited upside and pays no dividend
Pays a fixed dividend and has priority over common in liquidation
questions.explain: Preferred stock pays a stated dividend and ranks ahead of common equity in liquidation. It usually has no maturity date.

questions.q: Ginnie Mae mortgage pass-through securities are backed by:
choices: The full faith and credit of the U.S. government
questions.explain: Ginnie Mae guarantees are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, unlike Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac securities.

questions.q: Compared with an ETF, an exchange-traded note (ETN) carries:
choices: No credit risk because it holds the assets directly
Credit risk of the issuer, since it is unsecured debt
questions.explain: An ETN is an unsecured debt obligation of its issuer, so investors face the issuer's credit risk. An ETF holds the underlying assets.

questions.q: A principal-protected structured note's guarantee is ultimately backed by:
questions.explain: Structured notes are debt of the issuer, so the principal protection is only as strong as the issuer's credit.

questions.q: Which product is generally FDIC insured?
questions.explain: Bank deposits are FDIC insured. Mutual fund shares, money market fund shares and annuities are not.

questions.q: The New York Stock Exchange is best described as:
choices: A dealer market with no central location
An auction market with designated market makers
A market that lists only bonds
questions.explain: The NYSE uses a centralized auction process with designated market makers. Nasdaq is the dealer-style market in this comparison.

questions.q: Which order type guarantees a price but not execution?
questions.explain: A limit order executes only at the limit price or better, so it may never fill. A market order fills but not at a guaranteed price.

questions.q: Once its stop price is reached, a stop-loss order becomes:
choices: A limit order at the stop price
questions.explain: A stop order converts to a market order when triggered, so the fill price may differ from the stop price.

questions.q: A short sale profits when the stock price:
questions.explain: The investor borrows shares, sells them, and buys them back later. A falling price produces a gain.

questions.q: Under Regulation T, the initial margin requirement for buying stock on margin is:
questions.explain: Reg T sets initial margin at 50% of the purchase price. The 25% figure is the FINRA maintenance minimum, which is the trap.

questions.q: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a:
questions.explain: The DJIA weights each stock by share price, so high-priced stocks move it more than their market size would suggest.

questions.q: The S&P 500 index is weighted by:
questions.explain: The S&P 500 is a float-adjusted market-capitalization index.

questions.q: The ask price is the price at which:
choices: A dealer will buy a security from an investor
A dealer will sell a security to an investor
The security's par value is set
questions.explain: The ask is what the investor pays. The bid is what the investor receives when selling, and the gap between them is the spread.

questions.q: A Level 1 market-wide circuit breaker is triggered when the S&P 500 falls by:
questions.explain: Level 1 is a 7% decline before 3:25 p.m. Eastern, which produces a 15-minute halt. Level 3 (20%) halts trading for the rest of the day.

questions.q: A stock trading at $80 with earnings of $4 per share has a P/E ratio of:
questions.explain: P/E = price / earnings per share = 80 / 4 = 20. Dividing the other way gives 0.05.

questions.q: In a corporate bankruptcy, which group is paid before common shareholders?
choices: No one; common shareholders are paid first
questions.explain: Creditors, including bondholders, rank ahead of all equity holders. Preferred stock ranks ahead of common but behind creditors.

questions.q: Common stock dividends are:
choices: Declared at the discretion of the board and not guaranteed
Required by the Securities Act of 1933
questions.explain: Common dividends are discretionary and can be cut or eliminated. Preferred dividends are usually stated in advance.

questions.q: Over long historical periods, which asset class has generally shown the highest volatility?
questions.explain: Common stocks have historically had the highest returns and the highest volatility of these options.

questions.q: Preferred shareholders typically have:
choices: Veto power over all board decisions
questions.explain: Preferred stock usually carries limited or no voting power, which is the trade-off for its priority and fixed dividend.

questions.q: Compared with direct real estate, publicly traded common stock is generally:
questions.explain: Listed shares can be sold within seconds during trading hours. Direct property sales can take months.

questions.q: A mutual fund's net asset value (NAV) per share is calculated:
choices: Only at the time of each share purchase
Once daily, after the market close
questions.explain: Open-end funds price shares once per day, after the close, by dividing net assets by shares outstanding.

questions.q: A front-end load is:
choices: A fee charged when shares are redeemed
A sales charge deducted when shares are purchased
questions.explain: A front-end load is paid at purchase, which reduces the amount actually invested. A back-end load is charged on redemption.

questions.q: A 12b-1 fee is used to pay for:
choices: Fund audits required by the SEC
questions.explain: 12b-1 fees, named for the SEC rule, cover distribution and marketing costs and are part of the expense ratio.

questions.q: A fund with a 1.2% expense ratio costs an investor with $10,000 invested about how much per year?
questions.explain: 1.2% of $10,000 is $120. The trap is moving the decimal point to get $12.

questions.q: Compared with actively managed funds, index funds generally have:
choices: Lower expense ratios and lower turnover
Higher expense ratios and higher turnover
questions.explain: Index funds track a benchmark with little trading, which keeps costs and turnover low.

questions.q: A mutual fund's capital gains distribution that is reinvested is:
choices: Not taxable until the shares are sold
Taxable in the year it is distributed
Taxed only at the state level
questions.explain: Reinvested distributions are still taxable income in the year paid. Reinvesting does not defer the tax.

questions.q: Breakpoints in mutual fund sales charges:
choices: Reduce the front-end load on larger purchases
Increase the load for larger purchases
questions.explain: Breakpoints lower the sales charge percentage once a purchase reaches set dollar thresholds.

questions.q: Open-end mutual fund shares are redeemed at:
choices: The offering price including the load
The next calculated net asset value
questions.explain: Redemptions are priced at the next NAV after the request, not at the last trade or the original purchase price.

questions.q: Class C mutual fund shares typically carry:
choices: A large front-end load and no ongoing fees
A level annual 12b-1 fee and a contingent deferred sales charge for early redemption
Lower expense ratios than Class A shares
questions.explain: Class C shares have no front-end load but higher ongoing 12b-1 fees, and a short-term redemption charge applies.

questions.q: A fund with high portfolio turnover is most likely to generate:
choices: More short-term capital gains taxed as ordinary income
questions.explain: Assets held one year or less produce short-term gains, which are taxed at ordinary income rates. This raises the fund's tax cost for shareholders.

questions.q: When market interest rates rise, the price of an existing fixed-rate bond generally:
questions.explain: Bond prices move inversely to rates, because existing bonds must fall in price to match the yield on newly issued bonds.

questions.q: A $1,000 par bond with a 5% annual coupon pays annual interest of:
questions.explain: 5% of $1,000 par is $50 per year.

questions.q: A $1,000 par, 5% coupon bond trades at $950. Its current yield is closest to:
questions.explain: Current yield = $50 / $950 = 5.26%. The 5.00% figure is the coupon rate, not the current yield.

questions.q: Holding other factors equal, which bond has the greatest sensitivity to interest rate changes?
choices: Bond with a high coupon and short maturity
questions.explain: Long maturity and no interim coupons give a zero-coupon bond the highest duration and so the highest price sensitivity.

questions.q: A zero-coupon bond is typically sold:
choices: At a premium with semiannual coupons
At a discount to par, with no periodic interest
Only at auction at face value plus accrued interest
questions.explain: Investors earn the difference between the discounted purchase price and par at maturity, since no interest is paid along the way.

questions.q: Under standard rating scales, which rating is investment grade?
questions.explain: BBB- (S&P) and Baa3 (Moody's) are the lowest investment-grade ratings. BB+ is the first speculative grade.

questions.q: Interest from U.S. Treasury bonds is exempt from:
questions.explain: Treasury interest is taxable federally but exempt from state and local income taxes. Gains on sale are still taxable.

questions.q: A callable bond's main risk to the investor is:
choices: The issuer may redeem early when rates fall, forcing reinvestment at lower rates
Interest rate risk with no reinvestment risk
Loss of principal to inflation-indexed adjustments
questions.explain: The issuer redeems when rates fall, so the investor must reinvest the principal at lower yields. This is call risk combined with reinvestment risk.

questions.q: Yield to maturity assumes that:
choices: Coupons are spent and the bond is sold at par after one year
Coupons are reinvested at the YTM rate and the bond is held to maturity
Taxes are paid at the state level only
questions.explain: YTM assumes all coupons are reinvested at the same yield and the bond is held to maturity. Those assumptions often fail in practice.

questions.q: A bond with a coupon above current market rates trades at:
questions.explain: Investors pay more for the above-market coupon, so the price rises above par.

questions.q: A 5% coupon bond priced when market rates are 6% trades at:
questions.explain: A below-market coupon makes the bond worth less than par, so it trades at a discount.

questions.q: Reinvestment risk is greatest for a bondholder when:
choices: Interest rates rise and the investor holds a long bond
Interest rates fall after coupons are received
The bond is a zero-coupon issue held to maturity
questions.explain: Falling rates force coupons to be reinvested at lower yields. Zero-coupon bonds avoid this risk because they have no coupons to reinvest.

questions.q: Which bond has the highest interest rate risk?
choices: A 5-year coupon bond with a high coupon
questions.explain: The longest-duration bond has the most price sensitivity to rate changes. Floating-rate notes reset their coupons, so their price sensitivity is low.

questions.q: A general obligation municipal bond is backed primarily by:
choices: A bank letter of credit only
Revenue from a specific toll road
questions.explain: GO bonds are backed by the issuer's full taxing power. Revenue bonds rely on the revenue of a specific project.

questions.q: In bankruptcy, which debt ranks highest?
questions.explain: Secured creditors with collateral are paid first, ahead of unsecured and subordinated debt, and well ahead of equity.

questions.q: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) adjust their:
choices: Principal based on changes in the CPI
questions.explain: TIPS principal rises and falls with the CPI, and coupons are paid on the adjusted principal.

questions.q: A floating-rate note's coupon typically:
choices: Is fixed for the bond's life
Resets periodically to a benchmark rate plus a spread
questions.explain: The coupon follows a benchmark such as SOFR plus a fixed spread, which keeps the price close to par.

questions.q: A bond ladder reduces risk by:
choices: Staggering maturities so bonds mature at regular intervals
Holding only zero-coupon bonds of one maturity
questions.explain: Staggered maturities let the investor reinvest a portion regularly, which smooths the effect of rate changes.

questions.q: A bond bought between coupon dates settles with the buyer paying:
choices: The clean price plus accrued interest to the seller
Nothing extra; the seller keeps the accrued interest
questions.explain: The buyer pays accrued interest to the seller, who earned it, and the buyer collects the full coupon later.

questions.q: A bond's price is most likely to rise when:
choices: Market yields for similar bonds fall
The issuer's credit rating is downgraded
Market yields for similar bonds rise
questions.explain: Falling market yields raise the value of existing fixed coupons. Rating downgrades and inflation expectations generally push yields up.

questions.q: A call option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to:
choices: Buy the underlying at the market price only
Sell the underlying asset at the strike price
Buy the underlying asset at the strike price
questions.explain: A call is the right to buy at the strike. The put is the right to sell at the strike.

questions.q: A put option gives the holder the right to:
choices: Sell the underlying asset at the strike price
questions.explain: A put is the right to sell at the strike price, which gains value when the underlying falls.

questions.q: A call with a $50 strike on a stock trading at $55 has an intrinsic value of:
questions.explain: Intrinsic value of a call = max(stock price - strike, 0) = $5.

questions.q: A covered call strategy involves:
choices: Buying a put on shares you do not own
Owning shares and selling a call on those shares
Buying calls on shares you are short
Short selling shares and buying calls
questions.explain: The shares you own cover the obligation if the call is exercised. The strategy limits upside in exchange for premium income.

questions.q: Futures positions are marked to market:
choices: Daily, with gains and losses settled through margin accounts
Only when the contract is delivered
questions.explain: Daily settlement is a defining feature of futures and is what distinguishes them from forwards.

questions.q: Compared with futures contracts, forward contracts are typically:
questions.explain: Forwards are customized private agreements with counterparty risk. Futures are standardized and cleared.

questions.q: An investor who owns stock and buys a put on that stock is using a:
questions.explain: The put sets a floor on the value of the held shares, which is the definition of a protective put.

questions.q: All else equal, an option's time value:
questions.explain: Time decay (theta) erodes time value as expiration nears, and the decay accelerates near expiry.

questions.q: An investor buys 100 shares at $100 and a $100 strike put for $4 per share. If the stock falls to $60 at expiration, the net loss per share is:
questions.explain: The put pays $40, which offsets the $40 share loss. The only net cost is the $4 premium, so the loss is $4 per share.

questions.q: A wheat farmer who sells wheat futures to lock in a price is acting as a:
questions.explain: A hedger uses futures to reduce exposure to an existing price risk. A speculator takes on risk for profit.

questions.q: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was created by which act?
questions.explain: The Exchange Act of 1934 created the SEC. The 1933 Act governs new issues and the registration of securities.

questions.q: The Securities Act of 1933 primarily requires:
choices: Licensing of individual investment advisers only
Registration and prospectus disclosure for new securities offerings
questions.explain: The 1933 Act is the primary-market law: issuers register offerings and provide a prospectus.

questions.q: FINRA is best described as:
questions.explain: FINRA is a private, SEC-overseen self-regulatory organization for broker-dealers and registered representatives.

questions.q: SIPC protects customers of a failed brokerage up to:
choices: $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 in cash
questions.explain: SIPC covers missing securities and cash up to $500,000, of which cash is capped at $250,000. It does not protect against market losses.

questions.q: Regulation Best Interest requires broker-dealers to act in the:
choices: Best interest of the retail customer when making a recommendation
questions.explain: Reg BI raises the standard for retail recommendations above suitability, requiring the broker to put the customer's interest first at the time of the recommendation.

questions.q: Which SEC rule is the general antifraud provision most often used to prosecute insider trading?
questions.explain: Rule 10b-5 prohibits fraud in connection with securities trading and is the basis for most insider trading cases.

questions.q: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 requires CEOs and CFOs to:
choices: Own at least 5% of company stock
Certify the accuracy of periodic financial reports
Refrain from serving on the audit committee
questions.explain: SOX Section 302 and 906 require personal certification of periodic reports, with criminal penalties for false certifications.

questions.q: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, registered investment advisers owe clients:
choices: A duty only when managing retirement accounts
questions.explain: Advisers owe a fiduciary duty of loyalty and care. The suitability standard is the lower broker-dealer standard, which is the trap.

questions.q: The Investment Company Act of 1940 primarily regulates:
choices: Mutual funds and other investment companies
questions.explain: The 1940 Investment Company Act sets the rules for mutual funds, closed-end funds and UITs.

questions.q: State securities laws are commonly called:
questions.explain: Blue sky laws are state-level securities regulations, which supplement federal law. The name comes from fraud that was said to sell 'blue sky'.

vocab.def: The degree of investment loss an investor is willing and able to accept in pursuit of higher returns.
The length of time an investor expects to hold an investment before needing the money.
Spreading investments across assets so that losses in one holding are offset by others.
Market-wide risk that affects nearly all investments and cannot be removed by diversification.
Risk specific to one company or industry that can be reduced through diversification.
How quickly an asset can be converted to cash without a significant loss in value.
The division of a portfolio among asset classes such as stocks, bonds and cash based on goals and risk tolerance.
An individual retirement account funded with after-tax dollars, where qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
An individual retirement account that may allow tax-deductible contributions, with withdrawals taxed as ordinary income.
A U.S. tax rule that disallows a loss if a substantially identical security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale.
A dividend that meets holding-period and issuer requirements and is taxed at long-term capital gains rates.
A tax-advantaged education savings plan in which earnings grow tax-deferred and qualified withdrawals are federally tax-free.
The adjustment of an inherited asset's cost basis to its fair market value at the date of the owner's death.
A fund whose shares trade on an exchange throughout the day at market prices, typically tracking an index.
A mutual fund investing in short-term, high-quality debt that seeks to maintain a stable $1.00 net asset value.
A bank time deposit with a fixed term and interest rate, with early withdrawal usually subject to a penalty.
An insurance contract whose payments depend on the investment performance of chosen subaccounts, so the owner bears the market risk.
A company that owns income-producing real estate and must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders.
A fund that gradually shifts its asset allocation toward more conservative investments as its target retirement date approaches.
A fixed, unmanaged portfolio of securities that is sold in units and terminates on a stated date.
An investor who meets SEC Regulation D financial thresholds, such as net worth over $1 million excluding the primary residence, and may buy certain private offerings.
An unsecured debt security whose return tracks an index, so the investor bears the issuer's credit risk.
A regulated marketplace where securities are listed and traded through an auction or dealer process.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price, guaranteeing execution but not the exact price.
An order to buy or sell only at a specified price or better, guaranteeing the price but not execution.
An order that becomes a market order to sell once the stock falls to a specified stop price.
The sale of borrowed shares in the expectation of buying them back at a lower price to return to the lender.
A brokerage account that lets an investor borrow from the broker to buy securities, with the securities as collateral.
A market-wide trading halt triggered when a major index falls by set percentages, designed to slow panic selling.
An equity security representing ownership in a corporation, with voting rights and residual claim on assets after creditors and preferred holders.
An equity security that pays a stated dividend and ranks ahead of common stock in dividends and liquidation, usually with limited voting rights.
Preferred stock that requires any missed dividends to be paid in full before common shareholders receive dividends.
A mutual fund's total assets minus liabilities divided by shares outstanding, calculated once daily after the market close.
A sales charge deducted from the amount invested when shares are purchased.
A contingent deferred sales charge paid when shares are redeemed, often decreasing the longer shares are held.
An annual fee taken from fund assets to pay for marketing and distribution, included in the expense ratio.
The annual percentage of a fund's assets used to pay operating and management costs.
A dollar investment level at which the sales charge on a mutual fund purchase is reduced.
The face value of a bond, typically $1,000, which is repaid to the holder at maturity.
The fixed annual interest rate a bond pays, stated as a percentage of its par value.
A bond's annual coupon income divided by its current market price.
The annual return a bond earns if held to maturity with all coupons reinvested at the same rate.
A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes, expressed in years.
A bond that pays no periodic interest and is sold at a discount to par, with the return realized at maturity.
A bond that the issuer may redeem before maturity, usually when interest rates have fallen.
A bond rated BBB- or higher by S&P (Baa3 or higher by Moody's), considered to have relatively low default risk.
The risk that cash flows such as coupons will have to be reinvested at lower rates than the original yield.
A portfolio of bonds with staggered maturities so that portions mature at regular intervals.
A contract giving the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at the strike price before or at expiration.
A contract giving the holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying asset at the strike price before or at expiration.
The amount by which an option is in the money, such as the stock price minus the strike for a call.
An options strategy in which the investor owns shares and sells a call against them to earn premium income.
A standardized, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date, marked to market daily.
A strategy of owning shares and buying a put on them to set a floor on losses.
The federal law requiring registration and prospectus disclosure for most new public securities offerings.
The federal law that created the SEC and regulates secondary trading, exchanges and broker-dealers.
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, a self-regulatory organization that oversees broker-dealers and registered representatives.
The Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which protects customers up to $500,000 if a brokerage fails, including up to $250,000 in cash.
An SEC rule requiring broker-dealers to act in the best interest of a retail customer when making a recommendation.
State-level securities laws that require registration and antifraud protection in addition to federal regulation.
